cues.text: Let us turn now to the final topic of this session: global ethical governance.
When we talk about governing artificial intelligence, it is tempting to imagine a single rulebook.
In reality, AI governance is a layered collection of instruments.
It may include laws, regulatory guidance, professional codes, organisational policies, technical standards, and international recommendations.
These do not all carry the same weight.
A law is enforceable by the state.
A professional code binds members of a profession.
An organisational policy binds people within that organisation.
A technical standard describes an agreed way of doing something.
And an international recommendation sets out shared expectations that countries and institutions are encouraged to follow.
Keeping these layers distinct is the first skill in this topic.
Now let us look at the major examples the source gives us, one at a time.
First, UNESCO's recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence.
It emphasises human rights, dignity, fairness, transparency, environmental and social well-being, and oversight.
Notice that this is a recommendation.
It sets out values and expectations, rather than creating a statute that a court would enforce in the same way.
Second, the OECD AI principles.
These promote trustworthy AI, human-centred values, robustness, and accountability.
Again, think of these as principles that guide governments and organisations, not as a binding law in themselves.
Third, the European Union's AI Act.
This one is different in kind, because it is a regulatory structure, and it adopts a risk-based approach.
The idea of risk-based regulation is that the level of obligation is tied to the level of risk an AI system presents.
But the source adds an important qualification, and we must keep it: the applicability of the Act, its classifications, and its phased obligations require current legal verification.
So as a student, you should not rely on a summary, including this lecture, to tell you exactly which obligations apply to a given system today.
You verify against the current legal text.
Fourth, and closest to home, Nigeria's NDPA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act.
It governs personal data within its scope.
The phrase "within its scope" matters.
The NDPA does not cover everything about AI.
And the source also reminds us that sector-specific and other applicable rules may matter as well.
So an AI system handling personal data in Nigeria must be assessed under the NDPA, but you should also ask whether any sector or other rules apply.
Now the caution that ties all of this together.
Do not treat voluntary principles as binding statutes, and do not assume that one global law applies everywhere.
The UNESCO recommendation and the OECD principles are voluntary.
The EU AI Act and the NDPA are legal instruments, each with its own jurisdiction and scope.
Confusing these categories is one of the most common mistakes in this field.
Ethics, professional expectations, organisational policy, and enforceable law are related, but they are not interchangeable.
So how does an organisation put all of this into practice?
The source lists a set of governance measures.
Organisations should maintain AI inventories, so they know what AI systems they actually have.
They should carry out impact and risk assessments.
They should keep dataset documentation, recording what data is used.
They should perform model evaluation, testing how systems behave.
They should assign accountability roles, so that someone is clearly responsible.
They should apply access controls, limiting who can use or change systems and data.
They should provide incident and complaint mechanisms, so that problems can be reported and handled.
And they should keep audit trails, so that decisions and actions can be reviewed afterwards.

The source also asks for multidisciplinary review, meaning people from different fields examine the system together, and for the inclusion of affected groups, the people who will actually live with the consequences of the system.
Next comes a principle of proportionality.
A high-risk healthcare or education system demands stronger evidence than a low-stakes recommendation tool.
Think about why.
In healthcare, an error could harm a patient's health.
In education, a flawed system could affect a student's assessment or opportunities.
A recommendation tool for, say, suggesting items to browse carries far less at stake, so the evidence required before trusting it is lower.
The greater the potential harm, the stronger the evidence we should demand.
Finally, a sober reminder.
Certification and governance documents support, but do not guarantee, ethical outcomes.
Having a policy on paper, or a certificate on the wall, is helpful, but it does not by itself make a system fair, safe, or accountable.
Ethical outcomes depend on how the system is actually built, tested, monitored, and corrected over time.
To bring this together: AI governance is layered, combining laws, guidance, codes, policies, standards, and international recommendations.
Voluntary principles are not statutes, no single global law applies everywhere, and the EU AI Act requires current legal verification.
Nigeria's NDPA governs personal data within its scope.

And inside organisations, good governance means inventories, assessments, documentation, evaluation, accountability, access controls, complaint and incident mechanisms, audit trails, diverse review, and stronger evidence where the stakes are higher.
